sections.h2: How does probate work in Texas when the estate includes a house?
sections.html:
Probate is the court step that confirms a will or otherwise establishes who inherits, and a Texas house usually cannot be sold cleanly until that step, or one of its shortcuts, is finished. The route depends on whether there is a will, how much the estate owns and whether anyone owes money against it.

The Texas State Law Library lays out the main paths: probating a will, a muniment of title, a small estate affidavit, an affidavit of heirship and a determination of heirship. Each one ends with a document that gets filed with the county clerk where the land sits. That recorded paper is what a title company looks for before it insures a buyer.

Texas does not run one statewide probate office. Filings go to the probate court or county court in a specific county, and the process is local even though the rules are statewide. An estate with a house in one county and a bank account in another may touch more than one courthouse.

sections.h2: What is the four-year deadline to probate a will in Texas?
sections.html:
A will generally has to be offered for probate within four years of the death, though a court may accept a later filing when the applicant gives an acceptable reason for the delay. The State Law Library probate guide states this window.

The clock matters for a house sale because a will that was never admitted does not give anyone legal authority over the property. Families sometimes sit on a signed will for years, then discover the house cannot be deeded to a buyer. If the four years are close to running out, talk to a probate attorney or the clerk of the court in the county where the person lived.

  • A valid will is written, signed and witnessed by two people. A handwritten (holographic) will does not need witnesses.
  • The application is usually filed in the probate court of the county where the person lived.
  • A later date can be accepted only if the court agrees the delay was excusable.

sections.h2: Which probate routes exist for a Texas house, and which is fastest?
sections.html:
A muniment of title or a small estate affidavit is usually lighter than full administration, but each has conditions. The table below summarizes the routes described on the State Law Library pages and the county clerk manual from the Texas courts.

Texas routes for passing a house to heirs or a buyer, from State Law Library and county clerk manual pages
RouteFits whenWhat gets filed
Probate with administrationWill exists and a personal representative must handle debts and assetsCourt order, then executor's or administrator's deed for the house
Muniment of titleWill exists, no debts other than real estate liens, no administration neededCourt order and the will, recorded with the county clerk where the property sits
Small estate affidavitNo will, no administration applied for, assets of $75,000 or less excluding the homestead and exempt propertyAffidavit approved by the court; homestead copy recorded with the county clerk
Affidavit of heirshipFamily needs a sworn statement of who the heirs areSworn statement filed with the county clerk; no law makes third parties accept it
Transfer on death deedOwner signed and recorded one before dyingAffidavit of death and death certificate recorded

No route is fastest in every case. The right one is the one whose conditions the estate actually meets.

sections.h2: What does a muniment of title do when you want to sell?
sections.html:
A muniment of title lets a will serve as proof of ownership without a court-supervised administration, and it only fits an estate that owes nothing beyond liens on real estate. The court admits the will and signs an order, and the order plus the will are filed with the county clerk of the county where the house stands.

For a seller, this is often the cleanest paper trail when the family agrees and there are no unpaid creditors. A buyer's title company can read the recorded order and see who took title under the will. If any unsecured debt turns up, the estate may need a full administration instead.

sections.h2: When can a small estate affidavit be used for a Texas house?
sections.html:
It can be used only when there is no will, no one has applied for administration, the assets are $75,000 or less not counting the homestead and exempt property, and every heir agrees. That is the test in Estates Code chapter 205 as summarized by the State Law Library.

The same guide says the estate must hold enough to pay its debts and must not include real property other than a homestead passing to a spouse or minor children. A court has to approve the affidavit, and a copy covering the homestead is recorded with the county clerk. The county clerk manual adds that the affidavit is sworn by two disinterested witnesses, that at least 30 days must have passed since the death and that no petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted.

  • A house that is not the homestead generally pushes the estate out of this route.
  • An heir who disagrees stops the affidavit.
  • Ask the county clerk which forms the local court uses.

sections.h2: Can an affidavit of heirship or a transfer on death deed replace probate?
sections.html:
Sometimes, but neither one binds a buyer or title company by law. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement filed with the county clerk, and the State Law Library notes that no statute forces third parties to accept it, so some buyers and lenders will not.

A transfer on death deed works differently because the owner signed it while alive. The State Law Library says it passes real property without probate, can be cancelled by the owner and must be recorded before the owner dies in the county where the property sits. After death, the heirs record an affidavit of death with the death certificate. A Lady Bird deed, the enhanced life estate form, lets the owner sell or mortgage without the beneficiaries' consent.

If none of these exist, the court routes above are the fallback. A determination of heirship and an order of no administration are the court-based options named in the guide.

sections.h2: Who signs the deed when the estate sells the house?
sections.html:
That depends on how title passed, and the State Law Library property deeds page spells out the pairing. An administered estate uses an executor's or administrator's deed, a muniment of title uses the court order and will, and a transfer on death deed uses the recorded affidavit of death and certificate.

The county cannot add heirs to the old deed on its own. The new instrument has to be recorded in the county where the house sits, and Texas requires the signature to be acknowledged before a notary or another authorized officer before the clerk can record it. Recording fees are set by statute: the county clerk manual lists $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, with extra records management, archive and technology charges that vary by county.

sections.h2: Does Texas charge an inheritance tax or change the property tax bill after a death?
sections.html:
Texas repealed its inheritance tax with Senate Bill 752 in 2015, effective September 1, 2015, according to the Comptroller's tax library. Property tax is the cost that continues, since the lien for each year attaches on January 1 and the owner on that date owes the year's tax.

Heirs who live in the house can still claim the homestead exemption. Heirs not named on a recorded deed give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation, as the Comptroller exemptions page describes. A surviving spouse who is 55 or older may keep the deceased spouse's over-65 exemption in certain cases. Ask the appraisal district for the current forms.

sections.h2: What should heirs check before listing an inherited Texas house?
sections.html:
Confirm in writing who has legal authority to sign. Many delays come from a missing court order, an unrecorded deed or a disagreement among heirs about whether to sell.

  • Find the will, if any, and note the date of death so the four-year window is tracked.
  • Ask the county clerk which probate court has the estate and what is already on file.
  • Look for a recorded transfer on death deed in the property records.
  • List liens, since a deed of trust or tax lien is paid out of the sale.
  • Pick the route that matches the estate: muniment, small estate affidavit or administration.

A title company can tell you what it needs before it will close, and an attorney can confirm which route fits.

faqs.q: How long do you have to probate a will in Texas?
faqs.a: Four years from the date of death, in general. The State Law Library guide says a court may accept a later application when the delay has an acceptable reason, so a will found late is not automatically useless.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Texas before probate is finished?
faqs.a: Usually not to a buyer with title insurance. A buyer needs a recorded document showing who owns the house, such as an executor's deed, a muniment order or an approved small estate affidavit, and a title company will ask for it.

faqs.q: Is there a dollar limit for the Texas small estate affidavit?
faqs.a: Yes, assets must be $75,000 or less, not counting the homestead and exempt property. The estate also needs no will, no pending administration and agreement among all heirs, plus court approval.

faqs.q: Does Texas have an inheritance tax?
faqs.a: No. Senate Bill 752 repealed the Texas inheritance tax effective September 1, 2015. Property tax and any federal tax rules still apply separately.

faqs.q: Where are inherited property documents filed in Texas?
faqs.a: With the county clerk of the county where the house is located. The clerk acts as county recorder, and the deed or court order must be signed and acknowledged to be recorded.
